title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataract-2 (CTRCT2), which can take several forms, with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC) on chromosome 2q33-q35.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 (CTRCT2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC).
checks.evidence_quote: a 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene has been found in one allele of each affected family member and is absent from both unaffected family members and unaffected controls
checks.explanation: Heterozygous (one allele) CRYGC mutation in affected members of an autosomal dominant cataract family.

checks.claim: CTRCT2 can take several forms, with or without microcornea.
checks.evidence_quote: the other phenotypes described in those studies showed Coppock-like cataracts, zonular pulverulent cataracts, lamellar cataracts, nuclear cataracts, and nuclear and microcornea cataracts.
checks.explanation: The paper lists several cataract forms caused by CRYGC mutations, some with microcornea and some without.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33-q35.
checks.evidence_quote: We have localized the cataracts to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 including the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
checks.explanation: The gamma-crystallin cluster, which includes CRYGC, lies in the 2q33-q35 interval.

paragraphs.text: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by heterozygous mutation in the CRYGC gene. The lens opacities vary in form. Reported types include Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus, zonular pulverulent cataract, lamellar cataract, and nuclear cataract. Some families also have microcornea, nystagmus, and amblyopia (Lubsen et al., 1987; Ren et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2012).

checks.claim: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by heterozygous mutation in the CRYGC gene.
checks.evidence_quote: a 5-bp duplication within exon 2 of the gammaC-crystallin gene has been found in one allele of each affected family member
checks.explanation: Autosomal dominant inheritance and a heterozygous CRYGC mutation are supported. The abstract does not call the cataract congenital.

checks.claim: The lens opacities in CTRCT2 vary in form.
checks.evidence_quote: there are four other mutations in CRYGC that have been associated with cataracts including Coppock-like cataracts (T5P), variable zonular pulverulent cataracts (5 bp duplication), lamellar cataracts (R168W), nuclear cataracts (R168W), and nuclear cataracts (C109X)

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. The authors examined 53 family members, and 28 of them had congenital cataracts. Of these patients, 19 eyes (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) were unilateral and 9 were bilateral. On detailed slit-lamp examination, the clinically unaffected eye of patients with unilateral cataract showed no lens opacity. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, through bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgery. When historic data on the unexamined members were included, the family had 48 affected members: 28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined. Scott et al. (1994) noted that hereditary cataracts are typically symmetric, and that this family showed apparently random expression of the gene as either unilateral or bilateral cataract.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) reported a 4-generation Chinese family with 6 affected members. The family lived in a relatively isolated region of northern China. Affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, with a central nuclear opacity involving the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had congenital small eyeballs and corneas about 9 to 10 mm in diameter. No other ocular or systemic abnormalities were present. Every affected individual had the same poor visual acuity of hand movement in front of the eye, and all had nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) reported a 4-generation Chinese family with 6 affected members who had isolated bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and corneal diameter was about 9 mm in all affected individuals. The proband was diagnosed with bilateral nuclear cataract and microcornea at age 8 years and underwent iridectomy on both eyes at that age. At age 38, his left eye underwent phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation; best corrected visual acuity was 0.08 in the right eye and counting fingers at 30 cm in the left eye. Two other affected members were first diagnosed at 6 months and 1 year of age. Intraocular pressure was normal, and all patients had nystagmus and amblyopia. The family had no history of related systemic abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Lubsen et al. (1987) found 3 haplotypes (Q, R, and S) defined by polymorphic TaqI sites within the gamma-crystallin gene cluster in the Dutch and English population. They detected a fourth haplotype (P) in a family with Coppock-like cataract. Haplotype P was present in all affected family members and only in affected members. This showed close linkage between the cataract locus and the gamma-crystallin gene cluster (maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0).

checks.evidence_quote: Within the human gamma-crystallin gene cluster polymorphic Taq I sites are present. These give rise to three sets of allelic fragments from the gamma-crystallin genes. Together these restriction fragment length polymorphisms define eight possible haplotypes, three of which (Q, R, and S) were found in the Dutch and English population.

paragraphs.text: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned and characterized the gamma-D-crystallin gene and the gamma-E-crystallin pseudogene from the chromosome carrying Coppock-like cataract. The gamma-D gene worked the same as its wildtype allele. The pseudogene, however, had a cluster of sequence changes in and around its TATA box. Together these changes raised the activity of the pseudogene promoter 10-fold, bringing its expression to 30% of that of the gamma-D gene. The authors proposed that reactivation of the pseudogene, with overexpression of a predicted 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment, could cause the Coppock-like cataract.

paragraphs.text: Heon et al. (1999) found that the variant in the gamma-E-crystallin pseudogene previously reported as the Coppock-like cataract mutation was a polymorphism, present in 23% of their control population. Further analysis of the original Coppock-like cataract family showed a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of the CRYGC gene: a thr5-to-pro (T5P) substitution. The mutation was not seen in a large control population.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-generation family with autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataracts linked to 2q33-q35, Ren et al. (2000) sequenced the pseudo-gamma-E-crystallin promoter region. The results suggested that activation of the pseudogene was unlikely to cause the cataracts in this family. Base changes in the TATA box were also found in unaffected controls. Sequencing of the gamma-D-crystallin gene showed no abnormalities. In exon 2 of the CRYGC gene, however, the authors found a 5-bp duplication on one allele of every affected family member. The duplication was absent from unaffected family members and controls. It disrupts the reading frame and was predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin with 38 amino acids of the first 'Greek key' motif followed by 52 random amino acids.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract, Li et al. (2012) sequenced candidate genes and identified a heterozygous c.385G-T change in the CRYGC gene, resulting in a gly129-to-cys (G129C) substitution at a highly conserved residue. Molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies indicated that the mutation impaired the tertiary structure of the protein by modifying the hydrogen-bonding network in the C-terminal domain. The mutation markedly decreased the thermal stability of gamma-C-crystallin. It also substantially increased the protein's tendency to aggregate when stored at high concentration or exposed to heat or UV irradiation.

paragraphs.text: The linkage of Coppock-like cataract to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster reported by Lubsen et al. (1987) was the first genetic evidence that a lesion in a crystallin gene could be the primary cause of a human cataract. Brakenhoff et al. (1994) proposed that activation of the gamma-E-crystallin pseudogene caused the Coppock-like cataract. Heon et al. (1999) later found that the pseudogene variant was a common polymorphism and identified a CRYGC missense mutation in the original Coppock-like cataract family. Ren et al. (2000) also concluded that pseudogene activation was unlikely to cause cataracts in their family.
